lesson.title: The Five Plural Patterns
lesson.subtitle: Sort the taught nouns into -e, -er, -n, -s, and zero — then produce plurals in sentences

hook.title: Five Drawers
hook.content: German plurals have no single rule — they have five drawers, and every noun lives in one. Drawer -er (with umlaut): das Buch → die Bücher, der Mann → die Männer. Drawer -n/-en: die Frau → die Frauen, die Zeit → die Zeiten. Drawer -e: der Tisch → die Tische. Drawer -s: das Auto → die Autos (loans and snappy words). Drawer zero: der Lehrer → die Lehrer (no change). The good news: the drawers correlate with gender and shape — feminines overwhelmingly take -n, -er nouns take zero, monosyllabic masculines/neuters take -e or umlaut+e. Sort twenty-five nouns today and the drawers close themselves.

footnotes.title: The Plural Article Is Always die
footnotes.content: Whatever the drawer, the plural article is die — der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder. The plural erases gender: all nouns become die-words in the plural. The dative plural adds -n back (den Männern) — the only case that remembers the drawer.

pattern.title: The Sorting Tray
pattern.content: Tray -er (umlaut): Bücher, Männer, Häuser, Töchter, Kinder (no umlaut — the vowel never had an i). Tray -n/-en: Frauen, Zeiten, Zeitung-en? — die Zeitungen! -ung nouns take -en. Tray -e: Tische, Apfel? — die Äpfel (umlaut + e!), Gärten (umlaut). Tray -s: Autos, Fotos, Kaffees? rare — Handys (your trap-word takes -s!). Tray zero: Lehrer, Fernseher, Meter? hint. The umlaut sub-rule: only nouns with a, o, u can umlaut — Zeit can't (no a/o/u), Mann can. Twenty-five nouns, five trays, one sort.
pattern.linguist_note: The -s drawer is the modern loan lane (Autos, Handys, Babys), and it is growing. German plurals are historically six or seven systems worn down to five — the -en feminine drawer and the zero -er drawer are the deepest fossils.

exercises.prompt: Sort the nouns — match each singular with its drawer:
exercises.target_answer: die Bücher, die Frauen, die Autos, die Lehrer, die Spiele, die Stunden
exercises.meaning: the books, the women, the cars, the teachers, the games, the hours
exercises.explanation: -er umlaut, -n, -s, and zero — four of the five drawers, each with a family resemblance. Spiel and Stunde pick their drawers by sound.

exercises.prompt: Which noun CANNOT take an umlaut plural for phonological reasons?
options: die Zeit (no a, o, or u to umlaut)
exercises.target_answer: die Zeit (no a, o, or u to umlaut)
exercises.meaning: Umlaut needs a, o, or u
exercises.explanation: Umlaut pulls a/o/u forward. Zeit's i is already front — nothing to pull. Zeit → Zeiten, no dots. Sort the shelf: Blatt → Blätter (dots), Maus → Mäuse (dots), Vogel → Vögel (dots), Kuh → Kühe (dots), Auge → Augen, Ei → Eier, Knie → Knie — the vowels decide.

exercises.prompt: What is ALWAYS the plural article?
exercises.explanation: der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder, die Frau → die Frauen — the plural erases gender.

exercises.prompt: Drawer check: 'die Zeitung →' (the -ung nouns take which plural?):
exercises.explanation: -ung nouns are feminine, feminines take -n/-en: die Zeitungen. Two laws, one drawer.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The men find the books in the houses'
exercises.target_answer: Die Männer finden die Bücher in den Häusern
exercises.meaning: The men find the books in the houses

vocab_hints.note: dative plural adds -n: die Häuser → den Häusern — the case that remembers the drawer

exercises.explanation: Three umlaut plurals (Männer, Bücher, Häusern) — and the dative -n on Häusern is the drawer's receipt.

summary.outcome: Sort nouns into the five plural drawers and produce dative-plural -n correctly.

use_example.german: Die Männer finden die Bücher in den Häusern.
use_example.english: The men find the books in the houses.

summary.takeaway: Five drawers (-er/-e/-n/-s/zero), plural always die, dative plural adds -n — sort once, plural forever.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Twin Suppletions — gut/besser and good/better, the shared irregular story.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from The Five Plural Patterns (The men find the books in the houses):
twist.target_answer: Die Männer finden die Bücher in den Häusern
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Männer finden die Bücher in den Häusern" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of The Five Plural Patterns without relying on short-term echo.

mann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mann- — the identical twin of man; German keeps the short a English lengthened. [wiktionary]

frau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawjǭ 'lady, mistress' — kin to archaic English frow 'lady'; Fräulein andMs.-style Frauennamen carry the same root. [wiktionary]

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

spiel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spil 'dance'; no English cognate — English spiel is borrowed FROM German. [wiktionary]

stunde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stundu — cognate with archaic English stound 'hour'. [wiktionary]

blatt.context_translation: The leaf falls from the tree.
blatt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *bladą 'leaf' — English blade is the same word, meanings split. [wiktionary]

ei.context_phrase: Ich esse ein Ei zum Frühstück.
ei.context_translation: I eat an egg for breakfast.
ei.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *aij — Wiktionary lists English ey and egg as cognates. [wiktionary]

knie.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *knewą — the identical twin of English knee (silent k in both). [wiktionary]

vogel.context_translation: The bird sings in the garden.
vogel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, likely from 'to fly' — cognate with English fowl. [wiktionary]

kuh.context_phrase: Die Kuh steht auf der Weide.
kuh.context_translation: The cow stands in the meadow.
kuh.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōz, PIE *gʷṓws — the twin of English cow. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
